chatStore
owns the WS lifecycle
file: frontend/chatStore.ts

role.title: chatStore
role.text: Owns the WebSocket's entire lifecycle — opens it, sends frames, closes it — and republishes state to whatever UI subscribes. A plain TS class (subscribe/notify); no MobX/Redux required.

role.text: The three non-realtime reads: the room list (with unread counts), paginated history, and marking a room read. Same store, same auth token — fetch() instead of a socket.

1 · accept()
the ONLY yield point — first
file: chat_router.py

role.title: accept()
role.text: The only await/yield point in the whole handshake, and it now runs first — unconditionally, before any check. A real ASGI server discards a close code sent before accept() (a bare HTTP 403 instead), which is why this must come before the checks below rather than after.

label.text:
2 · Authenticate (sync)
verify JWT
file: auth.py

role.title: Authenticate
role.text: Verifies the JWT passed as a query param — a browser can't attach a custom header to a WebSocket handshake, so the token travels there instead. Runs synchronously; invalid/missing/expired closes with code 4001.

label.text: unconditional

3 · Check membership
is_member() → close(4003)
file: membership.py

role.title: Check membership
role.text: The single call into the one shared trust boundary below. Not a member → close(4003). Because there's no await before this point, nothing can change access underneath it.

label.text:
auth ok → continue
(4001 now reaches the client)

4 · Register socket
with the broker
file: chat_broker.py

role.title: Register socket
role.text: Adds the now-authenticated, now-authorized connection to the broker's registry so it starts receiving this room's broadcasts.

label.text: member → continue

Why accept() is first:
real uvicorn discards a close code sent BEFORE accept() —
the client just sees a bare HTTP 403.
TestClient has no such limit — this only shows up against a real server.
One check, right after accept(), is now enough —
it's the only yield point, already before the checks, so nothing can interleave.

role.title: Why accept() is first
role.text: A real ASGI server (uvicorn) silently discards a close code sent before accept(), returning a bare HTTP 403 instead — invisible against Starlette's TestClient, which preserves it faithfully. Accepting first also retires the old post-register re-check: there's no yield point left between the membership check and registration for anything to interleave in.

role.title: POST /rooms/{id}/read

label.text:
1 rate-limit → 2 validate (non-fatal) → 3 persist → 4 publish (sender included)
Rate-limit BEFORE validating — else a garbage-frame flood dodges the cap entirely.

role.title: Message loop ordering
role.text: Per received frame: rate-limit check first, then validate, then persist, then broadcast (sender's own socket included). Rate-limiting before validation matters — otherwise a flood of invalid/oversized frames never spends any budget.

role.title: is_member()
role.text: Every privileged entry point — the handshake and all three REST routes — calls this one function, never re-implementing the rule per route. It's the one file meant to be rewritten for your app (a friends table, a project-members table, a paid-access flag...).

In-memory registry (single process) today →
Redis / NATS pub-sub later — same interface, callers unchanged.
Also force-closes a LIVE socket the instant membership is revoked:
revoke() calls broker.close_user() directly.

role.title: ChatBroker
role.text: register/unregister/publish/close_user behind one interface. In-memory and single-process today; swap in a Redis/NATS-backed implementation when you run more than one process, with no caller changes. Also the mechanism behind immediate revocation.

role.title: Room / Message tables
role.text: The only two tables this pattern needs. Storage-agnostic — SQLite here, but the same SQLModel Session API works unchanged against Postgres/MySQL.

label.text:
If your test harness gives each simulated WebSocket connection its OWN event loop (e.g. Starlette's TestClient, by default),
broadcasting between two connections open in ONE test hangs forever — a cross-event-loop await. Fix: share one event
loop/portal per test client. Production never hits this: one process serves every connection on one loop.

role.title: Two testing gotchas
role.text: Both are a test double disagreeing with the real ASGI server, in opposite directions. (1) TestClient is MORE permissive pre-accept — it preserves a close code sent before accept() that a real server discards, masking the HTTP-403 bug. (2) TestClient is LESS permissive on event loops — each simulated connection gets its own, so broadcasting between two connections open in one test hangs unless you share a portal.
